claims.source: Report to the President by the Commission on CIA Activities within the United States, June 1975, chapter 16, pp. 227-228, https://documents2.theblackvault.com/documents/rockefellercommissionreport-full.pdf
claims.text: The Rockefeller Commission's June 1975 report disclosed the death without naming him: 'on one occasion during the early phases of this program (in 1953), LSD was administered to an employee of the Department of the Army without his knowledge ... Several days later, he jumped from a tenth floor window of his room and died as a result.' Its footnote to that passage reads: 'There are indications in the few remaining Agency records that this individual may have had a history of emotional instability.'

claims.source: Report to the President by the Commission on CIA Activities within the United States, June 1975, p. 227, https://documents2.theblackvault.com/documents/rockefellercommissionreport-full.pdf
claims.text: The same report records the ruling that produced death benefits and the discipline that followed: 'The General Counsel ruled that the death resulted from "circumstances arising out of an experiment undertaken in the course of his official duties for the United States Government," thus ensuring his survivors of receiving certain death benefits. Reprimands were issued by the Director of Central Intelligence to two CIA employees responsible for the incident.' The 2012 complaint states the opposite on the second point, that the internal investigation issued no formal reprimands.

claims.source: Private Law 94-126, 90 Stat. 3006 (1976), quoted in full in Olson v. United States, No. 12-1924 (JEB), D.D.C., memorandum opinion of 17 July 2013, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-dcd-1_12-cv-01924/pdf/USCOURTS-dcd-1_12-cv-01924-0.pdf
claims.text: Congress compensated the family by private statute. Private Law 94-126, 90 Stat. 3006 (1976), directs payment of 'the sum of $187,500 each to Alice W. Olson, Lisa Olson Hayward, Eric Olson, and Nils Olson, in full settlement of all of their claims against the United States arising out of the death of Doctor Frank R. Olson in November 1953, if all of them waive any and all rights arising out of such death.'

claims.source: Gerald R. Ford, Statement on Signing the Bill Providing for the Relief of the Survivors of Dr. Frank R. Olson, 12 October 1976, https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/statement-signing-the-bill-providing-for-the-relief-the-survivors-dr-frank-r-olson
claims.text: President Ford signed the bill on 12 October 1976 and stated the administration's own position on the amount: 'Legislation to appropriate $1,250,000 to compensate the wife and three children of Dr. Olson for his death was supported by this administration. However, the Congress approved a measure calling for the payment of a total of $750,000 to these survivors.'

claims.source: Eric Olson and Nils Olson v. United States of America, Civil Action No. 12-1924 (JEB), United States District Court for the District of Columbia, memorandum opinion filed 17 July 2013, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-dcd-1_12-cv-01924/pdf/USCOURTS-dcd-1_12-cv-01924-0.pdf
claims.text: The 2012 suit was brought in the District of Columbia, not Maryland, and was dismissed in 2013 without reaching the merits: 'Concluding that most of the allegations are both untimely and waived by a prior settlement agreement, and that any timely or preserved claims fall outside of the United States' waiver of sovereign immunity, the Court will grant the Government's Motion.' The same opinion records that 'the skeptical reader may wish to know that the public record supports many of the allegations that follow, farfetched as they may sound.'

claims.source: Project MKULTRA joint hearing, 3 August 1977 (Turner statement and Appendix B); Rockefeller Commission report, June 1975; Ford signing statement, 12 October 1976; Olson v. United States, D.D.C., 17 July 2013, https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/sites/default/files/hearings/95mkultra.pdf
claims.text: The four opened records do not agree. The Rockefeller Commission and President Ford give a tenth floor window; the Church Committee text in the 1977 Senate print gives a tenth story window of the Statler Hotel and the death as 27 November 1953; Ford and the 2012 complaint give 28 November; the complaint gives thirteen stories at 2:30 a.m. The CIA told the Senate in 1977 that he 'leaped to his death from a hotel room window in New York City about a week after having unwittingly consumed LSD'.

claims.source: Danny Jones Podcast, ep. 100, 1 July 2021, 2:10:37 to 2:11:31
claims.text: On the Danny Jones Podcast, episode 100, 1 July 2021, at 2:10:37, Tom O'Neill said Eric Olson has spent his life arguing his father was thrown from a window at the 'Statler Hilton' in New York in 1953 rather than having jumped, and that the government's own position is that Olson was used in an experiment but died by suicide. The opened records name the Statler Hotel, and the murder allegation is the 2012 complaint's, dismissed in 2013 on timeliness, waiver and sovereign immunity rather than on its truth.

desc: This is the one death inside a compartmented American programme that the government conceded, compensated by statute, and then litigated over sixty years later, and it belongs on this board because the paper trail exists on both sides. Frank R. Olson, a civilian employee of the Army at Fort Detrick, was given LSD without his knowledge in a bottle of Cointreau at a CIA and Army meeting on 19 November 1953 and died in New York within about a week. The Rockefeller Commission disclosed the connection in June 1975 without naming him, and attached to its own account a footnote saying the few remaining Agency records indicate he may have had a history of emotional instability. Congress paid his widow and three children $187,500 each in 1976 in exchange for a full waiver, and President Ford signed it saying his administration had wanted twice that. In 2012 two of the children sued the United States alleging the death was a murder concealed for sixty years; the District of Columbia dismissed the suit in 2013 on timeliness, the 1976 waiver and sovereign immunity, while recording that the public record supports many of the allegations. Four opened records disagree about which floor he fell from, what day he died and whether anyone was reprimanded.
